Learning Objectives

  1. Define enzyme, substrate, active site, cofactor, apoenzyme, holoenzyme, and coenzyme.

  2. Explain the purpose of cofactors.

  3. Discuss how the active site contributes to enzyme specificity.

  4. Describe the reaction carried out by the six major classes of enzymes.

Introduction

In the last module, we introduced you to the biomolecule class of proteins. In this lesson, we are going to talk about a specific type of proteins: enzymes. You may wonder why we are getting an entire lesson devoted to enzymes. Well, that's because enzymes run our lives, literally. You are going to find that everything about us, every reaction in our bodies, every function and form that occurs, is controlled by an enzyme. Enzymes are known as catalysts-things that speed up reactions. They control the rate of our reactions, which really means they control if and when every reaction occurs, but more on that later. In this lesson, we will learn about the structure and basic functions of enzymes, as well as the classes of enzymes.

Let's start with a video that covers the structure and basic function, and then recap and expand from there.
Amoeba Sisters Enzymes overviewOpen on YouTube

Enzyme Structure

What did we learn in the video? Enzymes depend on a precise 3D structure. We will discuss the formation of that structure in detail in module 6, so we are just going over some basics here.

First, the enzyme structure is created by the folding of a long linear polypeptide chain. This folding is essential. It is not random, but rather precise and specific to the protein. As you can see in the image above, each protein has a different structure. In fact, the way the protein is folded determines the function and specificity. Denaturation - unfolding - or misfolding of the protein means it won't work.

Fun Fact: This folding is the conformation of lowest energy, meaning it is the most energetically favorable and therefore the natural state. This will make more sense after the next lesson where we learn about free energy. There have been studies performed where scientists purposely denature proteins, and every time the proteins will fold back into the exact same conformation, showing just how specific the conformation is for each protein.

Function

What this means is we actually cannot separate the structure of the protein from the function because if we change the structure, we change the function. As we mentioned, they are catalysts for reactions. To add, they are highly effective and specific catalysts; they can increase the rate of a reaction by more than a million times, but they can only do this for their target reaction, and they can only speed up reactions, not make reactions that were never going to happen sudden occur.

Enzymes are workhorses. They are not consumed or permanently modified during the reaction. They are simply facilitators of the reaction, creating optimum conditions for the reaction to take place.

NOTE: The enzyme may wear out or breakdown over time, causing it to be less efficient or functional. This is not the same as it being consumed.

As I mentioned before, if you control the enzyme, you control the reaction. This “imbues living cells the ability to simultaneously conduct and independently control a broad spectrum of biochemical processes.” We will talk more about regulation in lesson 4 of this module, as it is vital to life.

Active Site

So how does the folding contribute to the function? Well, it creates the active site mentioned in the video. This is the place the enzyme binds to its specific substrate(s), or reactant(s) it will act upon. In fact, this is the first step in the catalysis of the reaction is the binding of the enzyme of the enzyme and substrate to form the enzyme-substrate complex (ES complex).

It was once believe that the enzyme and substrate fit together like puzzle pieces or a lock and key; their shapes were perfect complements of each other, and when they bound their thermal stability was greater than that of the stand alone enzyme (again, more on this in the next lesson). It is now known that something much more complex occurs during the formation of the ES complex. The active site is specific and generally matches the shape of the substrate, but it adapts and really takes the form of the substrates once the two are bound, much like a glove accepting and forming around a hand. This is called an induced fit. The substrate induces a conformational change on the active site, and this in turn induces a reciprocal change on the substrate.

The enzyme is facilitating the chemical reaction taking place by providing the environment for the transformation. This can happen in a myriad of ways:

  • It brings the substrates into close proximity to each other
  • It places the substrates into optimal alignment
  • It can shield substrates from water and generate an environment whose polarity, hydrophobicity, and/or acidity is different from the surrounding cytoplasm.
  • It places pressure on bonds during the induced fit
    • In fact, the full completment of the enzyme-substrate interactions is formed only when the substrate is in the transition state between substrate and product.

Cofactors

Another thing mentioned in the video is that many enzymes depend upon the presence of additional molecules known as cofactors in order to function properly. While the precise role of the cofactor varies depending on the enzyme and the cofactor, in general, cofactors are going to extend the repertoire of catalytic capabilities beyond those afforded by the functional groups present on the amino acid side chains of the peptides alone. I want to break down the terminology for you here so you can follow along later as we talk about different cofactors:

  • An enzyme without its cofactor is an apoenzyme
  • The complete catalytic enzyme, with cofactor in tow, is called a holoenzyme
  • A coenzyme is an organic molecule, typically derived from a vitamin
    • Coenzymes are cofactors. Cofactors are not always coenzymes.
  • Tightly bound cofactors are known as prosthetic groups.
    • They can be bound by covalent or noncovalent bonds (vs other cofactors that are weakly bound)
    • They are often called helper groups and help to shuttle functional groups from one molecule to another.
  • Cofactors are not specific for a single enzyme. They can bind to various enzymes.

Classes of Enzymes

Now that we understand the basics on structure and function, let's watch a more detailed video. Professor Dave is going to spend the first five minutes going back over everything we just covered, and then he is going to introduce us to our final section: the classes of enzymes.
Professor Dave enzymesOpen on YouTube
As we saw, there are six major classes of enzymes, divided based on the type of reaction they catalyze.

1. Oxidoreductases

Catalyze redox reactions via electron transfer between molecules.

2. Transferases

Catalyze the transfer of functional groups (remember those from module 1, lesson 1) between molecules.

We will see these frequently in places such as amino acid synthesis/degradation where we have aminotransferases.

3. Hydrolases

Catalyze hydrolysis reactions, which are the cleavage of molecules (breaking of bonds) via the addition of water.

4. Lyases

Catalyze cleavage of bonds without water.

Usually C-C, C-O, or C-N.

Tends to remove atoms and form double bonds.

5. Isomerases

Catalyzes conformational or geometric changes.

Molecules are rearranged into different isoforms to prepare them for future interactions via movement of functional groups.

6. Ligases

Catalyze the joining of molecules.

Important in DNA replication.

Powered by ATP hydrolysis because they require energy.

Learning Objectives

  1. Define spontaneous reactions, nonspontaneous reactions, endergonic reactions, and exergonic reactions

  2. Explain free energy and how it can be used to determine whether a reaction is spontaneous or not

  3. Compare and contrast free energy, standard free energy, and biochemical free energy.

  4. Analyze the enzymatic impact on chemical reactions, specifically transition states, activation energy, equilibrium, and rate.

Introduction

As we just learned, enzymes speed up chemical reactions, but they can only act on reactions that were already going to happen. In chemistry, or biochemistry if you will, we call these spontaneous reactions, reactions that take place on their own “without the input of energy”.

So how do we know if a reaction is going to happen spontaneously or not? Well, that all depends on thermodynamics. In a nutshell, reactions can be spontaneous if they are energetically favorable (release energy) and/or entropically favorable (increasing disorder). In order to determine that, we are going to be looking at the Gibbs free energy, AKA free energy or G (for Gibbs), the thermodynamic measurement of the energy capable of doing work-the work being driving a chemical reaction in this case.

Gibbs Free Energy and Reaction Spontaneity

Specifically, what we need to look at to understand how enzymes work is the amount of free energy required to initiate the reaction (this is known as the activation energy), and the different in free energy from the products to the reactants. This is known as the change in free energy or ΔG, and is going to be what determines whether our reaction is spontaneous.

Let's consider a reaction:

A + B <----> C + D

In this reaction, only one direction will be spontaneous, whereas the other will not. If this reaction were wood + oxygen ---> ashes + CO2, we can clearly understand that the reaction would proceed spontaneously from left to right, but not right to left.

Let’s start with a video about free energy, and then go over some important concepts we need to know about it before we move on.

I have selected the simplest video and will use the simplest possible explanations to give you only the information you need to understand the basic function and kinetics of enzymes. Let's look at some key points from the video regarding free energy and chemical reaction spontaneity.

1. A reaction can take place spontaneously only if ΔG is negative.

“Spontaneously” in the context of thermodynamics means that the reaction will take place without the input of energy, and in fact, the reaction releases energy. This release reflects a loss of orderliness or increase in entropy. The more negative the ΔG, the greater the amount of disorder created.

If we go back to our example above, the ashes are more disordered than the wood, and energy was released in the form of heat.

Such reactions, spontaneous reactions, reactions that release energy, are said to be exergonic reactions. Think exer like exit. Energy is exiting, or leaving.

2. A reaction cannot take place spontaneously if ΔG is positive.

This seems pretty obvious given #1, but I thought we should talk about it anyway.

An input of free energy is required to drive such reactions. Ashes and CO2 will never randomly turn back into wood and oxygen. It would require significant energy and intervention for that reaction to occur because it is nonspontaneous.

These reactions, nonspontaneous reactions, reactions that consume energy, are termed endergonic reactions. Think ender, meaning within, sounds like enter, because energy is entering the reaction.

3. The ΔG of a reaction depends only on the free energy of the products minus the free energy of the reactants.

What this is really saying is that the path or mechanism of the chemical reaction has no effect on the ΔG. It is only the difference in the free energy from the end state as compared to the initial state that matters and nothing in between.

For example, the ΔG for the transformation of glucose into carbon dioxide and water is the same whether is takes place by combustion of a series of enzyme-catalyzed steps in the cell. Meaning, the enzyme has no impact on the ΔG. This once again reiterates that enzymes are not changing reactions from nonspontaneous to spontaneous.

In our wood burning example, think of the enzyme as an accelerant, such as gasoline, that might make the wood burn faster, but it doesn't change the end result of the burnt wood.

4. In a system at equilibrium, ΔG is zero.

As we just said, ΔG is the difference between the free energy of the reactants and the products. When a reaction is at equilibrium, there is no net change in the concentrations of the products and reactants, meaning they are being made at the same rates, so there is no difference, meaning there is no change in free energy at equilibrium.

Once the wood is burned, there is no more shift in energy. The transfer has already taken place.

5. The ΔG provides no information about the rate of a reaction.

A negative ΔG indicates that a reaction can take place spontaneously, but it does not signify whether it will proceed at a perceptible rate.

This is where enzymes come into play. Some reactions may naturally occur at rates so slow, they are essentially not happening. Enzymes can speed this rate up more than a million times.

6. The ΔG changes based on the environmental conditions.

While we are not discussing the thermodynamics that go into the free energy calculations, it involves measuring changes in both entropy and enthalpy. Reactions can occur spontaneously if they are energetically favorable (release energy - have negative change in enthalpy) and/or entropically favorable (increasing disorder - have a positive change in entropy).

The important thing to know is that environmental conditions can alter these results, pushing something to be more or less spontaneous. For example, we saw in the video that increasing or decreasing the amount of substrate will alter the ΔG. Pressure and temperature will also alter the ΔG.

Standard Free Energy

Ending on the last note there once again brings us to the same question as before: How do we look at a reaction and know if it will be spontaneous or not, know if an enzyme can act on it or not, especially given that our measurement is ΔG, and ΔG can vary depending on the environment?

This is where standard free energy comes into play. Scientists have adopted this term, abbreviated ΔG°, in order to be able to compare the free energy of reactions and evaluate them solely on the nature of the reactants and products, eliminating any environmental variations. In this case, they are holding all the other variable steady at "standard" condition rates. You don't need to know them, but standard conditions being defined as 1.0M concentration of products and reactants, temperature of 298K or 25°C, and pressure of 1 atmosphere.

Biochemistists take this even further. We are looking at reactions within the human body, so we really only care about conditions within the human body. That would be pH of 7 and water concentration of 55.5M. This term is ΔG°’, and is the term we care about and will focus on for the rest of this course when we are referring to standard free energy.

So, for the rest of this course:

-ΔG°’ = spontaneous/exergonic reaction

+ΔG°’ = nonspontaneous/endergonic reaction

Super Duper Important Note: Although we will use ΔG°’ moving forward, technically, it is is ΔG that determines if a reaction is spontaneous or not because is ΔG°’ is assuming the environmental conditions, which are not always steady even in our body. Think about it- a reaction in our stomach is not occuring in an environment with a pH of 7.

This is an important thing to know because if a reaction is nonspontaneous according to is ΔG°’, we can force it to be spontaneous by adjusting the concentration of the reactants or products, as mentioned in the video. This is done by coupling reactions, which we will visit in Module 3.

Activation Energy and Enzyme Mechanisms

Now that we understand how to tell if a reaction can be acted upon by an enzyme, let’s take a quick look at how the enzyme works. We will get into extensive details in the next lesson, but I want us to get a general sense before we move on from free energy.

I want us to go back to #3 from above where we said the path or mechanism of the chemical reaction has no effect on the ΔG. It is only the difference in the free energy from the end state as compared to the initial state that matters and nothing in between.

I know I said it before, but I want to say it again because it is important that you understand an enzyme cannot alter the laws of thermodynamics. Enzymes will alter the rate of the reaction, but not the equilibrium of the reaction or the ΔG. All they do is help a reaction get where it was already going faster.

So how do enzymes do this? Well, that takes us back to the other item we mentioned at the beginning: all reactions require a certain amount of free energy to start. That energy is the energy of activation. Even spontaneous reactions need a push. Think about our wood again. Our wood that burns so easily cannot burn without some initial heating element. In the case of our wood burning, that energy was a match or some other flame. Inside our cells, that push is enzymes.

As we mentioned in the last lesson, the enzyme and substrates will bind together to create an induced fit, which will form optimal conditions for the substrate, therefore facilitating the substrates reaching the transition state.

In a spontaneous reaction, the transition state is the highest energy point, meaning getting there is the part that requires the activation energy and everything beyond the transition state is downhill. Once the reaction is initiated, it will continue on its own.

Basically, enzymes work by lowering the amount of energy required to initiate the reaction. You can see this in the chart above and the video at the start of this section. Using an enzyme means less work is needed for the reaction to occur, and more substrates are in the transition state, so more products are formed.

Introduction

Now that we understand the thermodynamics behind reactions, we are ready to learn about enzyme kinetics. Kinetics is the study of the rates of chemical reactions, and enzyme kinetics is the study of the rates of enzyme catalyzed chemical reactions. We are going to start by learning about basic velocity of reactions.

Once again, this is a complicated subject, so I am sticking to the basics that we need to know for enzyme kinetics only. In my opinion, this is the most complicated lesson of the semester, and I boil it down to bare bones as much as possible. There is plenty more we could dive into here, so feel free to reach out if you are interested.

Velocity of Reactions

Let's consider the simple reaction

A ---> C

As we know, in this case, A is the reactant and C is the product.

First, what do we mean by the velocity of the reaction?

The simple answer is the rate of the reaction, yes, But, chemical reactions happen so fast, that it's not really helpful to put a timestamp on them. So instead, we refer to this as the quantity of reactant (A) that disappears in a specified unit of time. This way, we can designate the unit of time into something we understand, like one second. How much A disappears per second.

Note: Another way we could have defined this was the quantity of the product (C) that appears in a specified unit of time because if A is disappearing, C is appearing. We are going to speak in terms of reactants, and you will understand why as we continue.

Everyone still with me? Good. So, here comes the important part. In the reaction above, we can alter the velocity by changing the concentration of A (designated [A]). In fact, we do just that, and we put an equation to it:

V = k[A]

Where k is a rate constant specific to the reaction A---> C. This means k is unique for every chemical reaction.

This type of reaction, one where the velocity of the reaction is directly proportional to the reactant concentration, is known as a first order reaction.

Given that we just named that type of reaction, you can probably guess that we are about to get into a different type. Consider the following two reactions:

2A ---> C and A+ B ---> C

In these cases, we have two reactants instead of just one (either 2 of A or A and B), and the velocity is proportional to the product of the concentrations of the reactants. Our equation becomes:

V = k[A]^2 and V = k[A][B] respectively.

These are second order reactions.

Important Notes: If you weren't confused enough...

1. Sometimes when a second order reaction has reactants at varying concentrations, it will appear as a first order reaction because the rate will not appear to depend on the concentration of the reactant present in large quantities at all (One reactant is always available, so the reaction will only occur when the less available reactant is present, meaning the less available reactant controls the rate of the reaction)

Here is an example: Think about if you want to make Jello right this minute, which requires two reactants, water and a Jello packet. Technically, this is a second order reaction because it has two reactants. But, which of those two things would limit your ability to make the Jello? Water is always available. Even if you don't have it in your hand at the instant you need it, you can always get it when needed. So really, you can make Jello any time you have a Jello packet. Therefore, the reaction is only dependent upon the availability, or concentration, of the Jello packet, meaning it is acting like a first order reaction.

2. Under some conditions, namely incredibly high [reactant], a reaction can be zero order because the reaction is independent of the reactant concentrations. Enzyme-catalyzed reactions can approximate zero order reactions in some cases, as we will see shortly. Since we are going to talk about this more soon, I will hold off on giving you an example.

Michaelis Menten Equation

Now, let's add in an enzyme to our reaction.

All we are doing is setting the stage at this point. I want to be sure you understand the foundation before we dive in. But we haven't really talked about what we are diving in to at this point, so maybe it's time for me to explain that.

1. What are we trying to figure out? How the initial velocity (Vi) of an enzyme catalyzed reaction changes based on the concentration of a substrate (reactant).

2. Why? This will allow us to understand the standard operations of the enzyme, so we can then tell if the enzyme is operating outside of these norms (if there is a deficiency), which is what we will look at next.

3. How will we do this? The Michaelis-Menten Equation

The Basic Chemical Reaction

For this section we are going to switch our terms a bit. We will call the reactant the substrate (S), since that is what we use when an enzyme (E) is involved. You will also see the enzyme-substrate complex (ES) and product (P). So, our reaction for this section is as follows:

E + S <---> ES ----> E + P

Following the same process as above, lets add in our rate constants (k) to our chemical reaction:

k1 k2
E + S <---> ES ----> E + P
k-1

As we mentioned, rate constants are unique for each reaction, so we have 3 reactions and 3 rate constants:

  • k1 is the rate constant for E + S ---> ES
  • k2 is the rate constant for ES ---> E + P
  • k-1 is the rate constant for ES ---> E + S

If we combine all these together, we are going to get a new rate constant for this equation known as the Michaelis constant (Km).

Our calculation for Km, which I will not ask you to know, is:

k-1 + k2
Km =
k1

You will see it is also equal to the [S] that yields Vmax/2

Km is going to describe the properties of the enzyme-substrate interaction, and is specific for each enzyme-substrate combination.

The Assumptions

We are also making two assumptions for our equation here, just for simplicity sake:

1. We are treating this like a first order reaction only influenced by [S]. This is like our water and jello example from above, with our enzyme being the water and the substrate being the jello (although in this case the [S] is technically greater than the [E]).

2. The only driving force is the initial reaction (k1). We are operating under the assumption that, as we discussed before, the rate-limiting step for this reaction is the formation of the ES transition state, and once that is formed, everything else is downhill.

Note: There are ways to calculate when these two things are not true, but for this class, we will not be looking at anything that complicated.

The Abbreviations

Finally, before we jump into the equation, let me introduce you to the terms, so that when they come up, you are familar with them.

  • Km = Michaelis constant. [S] that yields half of Vmax
    • Unique to each enzyme-substrate combo and independent of [E]
  • Vi = Initial reaction rate
  • Vmax = Maximal reaction rate.
  • Kcat = Turnover number of the an enzyme. Vmax/[E]T
    • Given a fully saturated enzyme, it is the number of substrate molecules an enzyme can convert into product.
  • [E]T= Total enzyme concentration. [E] + [ES]

The Theory

In the body, our enzyme concentrations are tightly regulated. Protein synthesis happens pretty quickly, so we can create enzymes as needed, and we can turn them on and off or signal degradation as needed to ensure we have constant control of our enzymes. All of this is going to be covered later. What you need to know now is that the enzymes are like the water from our water and jello analogy - in this instance, they are not the part that will determine the initial velocity of the reaction.

The reason for this is because we know that enzymes speed up reactions, but in order to speed up the reaction, they first have to bind to the substrate, as we learned in the last lesson. So there needs to be a physical interaction between the enzyme and the substrate. Within a cell, molecules are bouncing around, and given a steady amount of enzyme, the more substrate molecules bouncing around, the higher the chance for ones to bounce into an enzyme.

The Equation

Ok, I think you are finally ready for the actual Michaelis Menten equation. Remember, this equation is calculating the intial rate of the reaction, showing how the enzyme activity varies as we adjust the substrate concentration:

Vmax [S]
Vi =
[S] + km

Let's start with an image to understand what we are talking about, and then we will continue on to a graph so we can do some interpretations.

Check out the three hotspots in the image below to learn more about the relationship between [S] and reaction rate.

• A. [S] < Km

    When the substrate concentration is low, much of the total enzyme concentration ([E]T) is in the free state (E vs ES).

    This means there is still plenty of available active sites, so adding more substrate will increase the rate of the reaction.

  • B. [S] = Km

    At the point at which the substrate concentration is equal to Km, we are at the shifting point for our enzyme. The addition of more substrate at this point will still increase the velocity of the reaction, although the rate of return will be smaller from this point on.

  • C. [S] > Km

    When the substrate concentration is high, the enzyme is going to be saturated, meaning [E]T = [ES].

    Adding more substrate at this point will do nothing to the velocity.

Lineweaver-Burk Plot

Determination of Vmax and Km for an enzyme catalyzed reaction is often one of the first characterizations of an enzyme undertaken. However, just as it is impractical to measure the rate of a reaction outright, so we therefore measure it as output per unit of time, we also cannot directly measure Vmax, and therefore we cannot directly calculate Km. If you know anything about a hyperbola, then you already know why. But in case you forgot your math, you can think of it in terms of perfection-Vmax is something that is approached, but rarely attained.

To directly measure Vmax would require impractically high concentrations of substrate in order to saturate the enzyme. Therefore, a linear form of the MM equation has been created to circumvent this issue and allow extrapolation of Vmax from the initial velocity data obtained at less than saturating concentrations of the substrate. This linear form is known as the Lineweaver-Burk plot, and while it is not often used since computers can extrapolate for us know, it is a basic biochemical concept, so we still need to go over it, even if briefly.

Catalytic Efficiency

There's one more thing I need to throw at you. We have talked this entire time about how we can assess the function of an enzyme using these parameters, yet we have neglected to account for variations in the enzymes themselves.

Remember, Vmax is the maximum rate of the enzyme catalyzed reaction, right? It only happens when all our enzyme is saturated with substrate. So, another way we can say this is the number of substrate molecules that an enzyme can convert into product per unit time when the enzyme is fully saturated with substrate.

Now, we are going to take this a step futher and we are going to measure the rate of catalysis (Kcat), which will be the Vmax divided up by the total number of active sites available in the reaction, so we can tell the catalytic rate for each active site individually.

Obtaining the rate of catalysis then, will allow us to determine the catalytic efficiency, which I swear is the very last thing you will need to know for this lesson.

So, here we go, one final measurement and set of standards. You can do it!

Our measurement: Catalytic efficiency

Our equation: Kcat/Km (once again unique to an enzyme-substrate combination)

The benefit: Takes into account both the rate of catalysis (Kcat) and the nature of the enzyme-substrate interaction (Km)

Our result: Specificity constant unique to an enzyme-substrate combination.The catalytic efficiency will allow us to compare the efficiency of different enzymes-substrate combinations. So we can see if an enzyme prefers one substrate over another, or if one enzyme could be a valid substitute for another, say for drug creation... Ahhhh... are we starting to understand why this is such an important topic yet?

Interpretation: The higher the specificity constant, the higher the affinity the enzyme has for that substrate.

Introduction

Enzymes tend to operate close to Km because this allows for control of reaction rates. Think about it- enzymes that operate at their maximal rate cannot increase throughput to accommodate surges in substrate availability and will reduce their output of product only if substrate concentration decreases precipitously.

As we will learn in the next module, we will need to be able to adjust our chemical reactions according to the needs of our cells. The easiest way to do this is by controlling the catalytic activity- control the enzyme, control the reactions. In the final lesson of this module, we will learn about the different ways to control enzymes, which will happen as a result of various cellular signals, and then in the next module you will see why this is so important.
Environmental Regulation

In general, an increase in temperature comes with an increase in chemical reaction rate due to an increase in molecular movement, and therefore an increased chance of interaction; however, once a certain temperature peak is reached, the enzyme efficiency drops off almost immediately. This is because the weak bonds that hold the enzyme’s structure in place are broken, causing the enzyme to denature. Different enzymes have a different optimum temperature range in which they operate most effectively. For biological enzymes, this is typically right around body temperature. This is why a high fever is so dangerous; increasing the body temperature causes denaturation of enzymes, which leads to breakdown of biological processes.

Fun Fact: The enzyme tyrosinase is responsible for pigmentation in Siamese cats. It in inactive at normal body temperatures, which is why the dark pigment is only found on the extremities and not the core of the cat's body.

Just as enzymes have an optimal temperature, they also have an optimal pH. While most enzymes in our body operate at a pH of 7.3-7.5, similar to that of our blood, there are many that are exceptions to this- particularly our digestive enzymes. Pepsin prefers the acidic environment found within lysozymes and our stomach, whereas Chymotrypsin prefers the basic environment of our intestine.

This allows for compartmentalization of activities more-so than timing control, and prevents our digestive enzymes from breaking down molecules outside of the target regions. We can't just have digestive enyzmes actively running amuk throughout our body after all, right?

Enzyme Level Control

Proteins are continuously synthesized and degraded. Most of the time, enzyme concentrations are held fairly constant with new enzymes being synthesized to replace those that are worn out and degraded. However, many enzymes are also controlled at the molecular level, with concentrations being altered on an as-needed basis. Cellular signals will induce or repress transcription factors that will control the amount of protein being synthesized. Likewise, the pathway for protein degradation, outlined in module 6, can be triggered if there is excess enzyme that needs to be removed.

This type of regulation is preferred when long-term adaptation is required, such as with a change in diet, exercise, environmental conditions, etc.

Catalytic Activity Control

The final way, and arguably the most common way, in which enzymes are regulated in through the control of the catalytic activity of the enzyme. That is, shutting the enzyme on and off at will. This is typically done by using other molecules that will stimulate or inhibit the enzyme.

This type of regulation is favored for rapid and transient alterations. Let’s look at this different options for enzyme control by other molecules.

Allosteric Regulation

What if I told you enzymes in our cells are not Michaelis Menten enzymes at all? Would you be mad at me for making you go through that entire lesson? Well, it’s true. The enzymes in our cells are more dynamic. They react to far more than simply substrate concentration. Many of our enzymes are known as allosteric enzymes. They are enzymes that will change their 3D shape in reaction to an effector molecule that will bind and control their catalytic activity. This effector molecule can be stimulatory or inhibitory. Let’s focus on the inhibitory methods in this case.

The allosteric binding site is typically not the same as the active site. It is a location where a molecule would bind to turn the enzyme on or off. Example:

Hemoglobin (a protein, but not actually an enzyme) carries oxygen throughout the blood. The effector molecule for hemoglobin is 2,3 bisphosphoglycerate, which controls the ability for oxygen to bind to hemoglobin. This makes sense.We need hemoglobin to bind oxygen in the lungs, keep it bound through the blood, and then release as needed in the tissues, so our bodies have developed a simple way to control this process.

Feedback Inhibition

The most common form of allosteric regulation will be feedback inhibition. As we will see in the next module, our metabolism is a series of chemical pathways. Let's consider the following reaction:

A ----> B ----> C ----> D ----> E

Each step in the process is controlled by a different enzyme.

Once a suffient amount of E is produced, there are several options:

  • Option 1: The pathway keeps going, and E keeps building up. This is a bad idea. It's wasteful and could be harmful.
  • Option 2: D---> E is shutdown because E is full. But now D starts to back up. So, then C ---> D gets shut down, and we just end up clogging up the whole pipeline.
  • Option 3: E goes back and inhibits the first reaction, A ----> B. Winner, winner!!!

E is often an allosteric inhibitor of the enzyme that runs A ----> B. This is a process known as feedback inhibition. It works just like your thermostat and your AC system. Once the temperature is cool enough, the cool air shuts the AC off.

Allosteric inhibitors, ones that don't bind to the active site, are only one example of inhibitors. Check out the video to learn about the 3 types of inhibitors and then we will chat.

• Noncompetitive Inhibitors (V-series Enzymes)

    Allosteric inhibitors that do not bind to the active site are examples of non-competitive inhibitors. In your book, they are known as V-series enzymes because they lower Vmax without affecting the Km. This is because a noncompetitive inhibitor does not prevent a substrate from binding to the active site, and remember, Km describes the properties of the enzyme-substrate interaction, which have not changed. What has changed, is that the reaction will not continue once they have bound.

    Important note: No amount of additional substrate will overcome a non-competitive inhibitor. Only release of the inhibitor will remove the effect. Certain poisons are so tightly bound that they are considered permanent inhibitors, once bound, they permamently incapacitate the enzyme.

    These are going to be the preference when it comes to a drug formation because the drug cannot be overcome by the substrate the drug is designed to counteract.

  • Competitive Inhibitor (K-series Enzyme)

    Another option is a competitive inhibitor, which is one that is shaped like the substrate and will compete for the active site. Your book calls these K-series enzymes because Km is raised without an effect of Vmax. This is because the catalytic activity of the enzyme has not been influenced, but it just doesn’t have as great a chance to interact with the substrate. In fact, the hallmark of a competitive inhibitor is that it can be overcome by a sufficiently high concentration of substrate.

    If we go back to our hemoglobin from before, an example of a competitive inhibitor is carbon monoxide. The reason someone can suffocate in a garage full of oxygen is because their hemoglobin will bind to carbon monoxide instead of oxygen, meaning they are not circulating oxygen through their body. The only way to overcome this and "correct" carbon monoxide poisoning is to saturate with oxygen.

  • Uncompetitive Inhibitor

    Finally, there is the option of an uncompetitive inhibitor. This is an allosteric binding site that blocks the active site, meaning it impacts both Km and Vmax. It can prevent binding of the substrate if the inhibitor is bound before the substrate, or it can allow the formation of the enzyme-substrate complex, but then prevent completion of the reaction if it binds after the substrate.
